W1-1.note: The search ends in disappointment that turns to a felt touch of hands with 'my little comrade of seasons long since dead'; the wondering in E is a passing moment, not the main concern.

W1-2.note: The capitalized words are examples of words that strike the 'chord' that 'never fails to thrill'; CAVE, TRAP-DOOR and SLIDING-PANEL are not riches, so D fits only half the list.

W1-3.note: The foreign coins are 'thicker and clumsier of make than those I hoarded myself,' so he kept coins; the buttons and egg list belong to the other boy.

W1-4.note: He calls him a 'kindred spirit,' a 'happy starred young person,' and 'my little comrade.'

W1-5.note: 'Some other boy, perhaps, would some day release that spring again. I trusted he would be equally appreciative.'

W1-6.note: The shouts and yells show a game of bears or bandits just getting started, which he will join 'in another minute'; the modern idiom 'time is up' makes C tempting.

W2-1.note: The narrative moves from 'a strange man' to 'He is a "strange man" no longer... He is my father'; E is contradicted by the ending, where the distance is overcome.

W2-2.note: The universe 'bounded by the wooded hills' and Granma Green's house on 'the very edge of the world' convey how small the child's world was.

W2-3.note: He submitted 'rather for the reason that my mother urged me forward than because of any affection.'

W2-4.note: She was 'two years older,' and the narrator 'had forgotten him' while the baby 'had never known him,' which implies that age and memory are what set her apart.

W2-5.note: 'Of her own motion' contrasts with the narrator, who went only because his mother urged him, so it means of her own accord.

W2-6.note: He still hears 'the sad reproach' and reflects that 'the war had in very truth come between this patriot and his sons.'

W3-1.note: They build the screen together and then 'turned to other things,' never returning to see whether the birds lived; C asserts an outcome the poem says they never learned.

W3-2.note: 'The cutter-bar had just gone champing over' it and 'left [it] defenseless to the heat and light.'

W3-3.note: The chicks rising as if to a mother bird long 'deferred' 'Made me ask would the mother-bird return.'

W3-4.note: The speaker fondly recalls the companion's play, offers to help, and shares the work and the memory ('have you?').

W3-5.note: 'Dared not spare to do' means dared not hold back from or leave undone; the common sense 'afford' does not fit this construction.

W3-6.note: 'All this to prove we cared. Why is there then / No more to tell? We turned to other things' expresses surprise that their concern stopped once the screen was up; the poem implies nothing about how the birds fared.

W4-1.note: The Labor Museum's exhibit leads Angelina to see her mother with a background other than the tenement, and to take pride in her.

W4-2.note: They could 'drop their spindles over the edge of a precipice,' which gave them skill beyond neighboring towns.

W4-3.note: 'Traditional... observances' to which 'her very religion clung' are customs and practices.

W4-4.note: The paragraph opens 'That which I could not convey to the child, but upon which my own mind persistently dwelt' and describes the mother being torn from everything she knew.

W4-5.note: She describes the mother as torn from her home and walking 'timidly but with poignant sensibility upon a new and strange shore.'

W4-6.note: 'The thought of her mother with any other background than that of the tenement was new to Angelina.'

W5-1.note: The passage argues that this little squirrel is the 'master-existence' and 'master forester,' and marshals facts to support 'the importance I ascribe to him.'

W5-2.note: 'Though only a few inches long,' he makes himself more important than even the huge bears.

W5-3.note: 'The greater portion is of course stored away for food to last during the winter and spring'; only 'some' are buried singly.

W5-4.note: He mentions the facts 'to show upon how substantial a foundation the importance I ascribe to him rests,' which anticipates doubt about so large a claim.

W5-5.note: 'Closely allied to' the Chickaree, and possibly 'a lineal descendant,' means closely related.

W5-6.note: The squirrel is 'by far the most interesting,' has 'fiery vigor,' and is 'the larger and more beautiful animal.'

W6-1.note: It opens with the question of why there is 'far less green vegetation' and answers it with the gas, acid rain, tephra and Kona winds.

W6-2.note: The 'dominant Northeast trade winds' carry the plumes southwest into the Ka'u Desert, away from public viewing areas.

W6-3.note: The readings come from samples 'collected downwind of Kilauea's summit during the lava lake days from 2008-2018,' not from 2026, and show how acidic that rain was.

W6-4.note: The author calls it 'a secret weapon' and 'the amazing capability.'

W6-5.note: The 'hearty native trees' are highly adapted survivors, so the word means sturdy or hardy.

W6-6.note: 'When it falls out of the eruptive plume it has enough energy to strip the foliage right off the trees,' even though it is light enough to float.
